DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26

The report has a sensible question, clear data and a cheap, plausible intervention. But it contains one factual error that reverses a headline claim, and its main conclusion goes further than the evidence supports. Both should be fixed before it goes to the Health and Wellbeing Board.

## 1. Overall uptake is wrong, and the "national ambition met" claim fails

The "All schools" row gives 13,772 vaccinated out of 22,080 eligible. That is **62.4%**, not 66.0%. The group figures confirm this: a weighted average of 70.0% (9,120 pupils) and 57.0% (12,960 pupils) is 62.4%.

So Eastvale was **below** the 65% national ambition, not above it "for the first time". This sentence in Section 3 needs to be corrected or removed. This matters for the Board: the argument shifts from "keep improving" to "we are still short of the target."

All other figures in Table 1 and Section 5 check out:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Reminder group | 70.0% uptake, 75.0% consent, 93.3% of consented vaccinated |
| Non-reminder group | 57.0% uptake, 61.5% consent, 92.7% of consented vaccinated |
| Column totals | Correct |
| Costs | 4,990 × 3 × £0.08 ≈ £1,198; 2,280 × 3 × £0.08 ≈ £547; plus £2,500 set-up ≈ £4,245, under £5,000 |

## 2. The 13-point gap is not evidence that reminders caused a 13-point rise

This is the central problem. Schools chose whether to opt in, and the report's own data show the two groups differ in ways that strongly affect uptake:

- **School nurses:** 29 of 38 reminder schools had a full-time nurse (76%), against 11 of 54 non-reminder schools (20%).
- **Affluence and geography:** reminder schools were mostly in the more affluent west. Non-reminder schools include the eastern wards, which have more families speaking other languages at home and more household mobility.
- **Contact data:** valid mobile numbers were held for 93% of families in reminder schools but only 61% in non-reminder schools.
- **Wide spread:** non-reminder schools ranged from 38% to 79%. Some schools without reminders beat the reminder-school average, so other factors clearly matter a great deal.

Opt-in schools may simply have been better-resourced, more engaged schools that would have done better anyway. The 13 points is the **total** difference between the groups. Some unknown share of it is due to reminders, possibly a small share.

Phrases to revise:
- "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points" (Section 3)
- "Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points" (Section 6)
- "more than any other intervention we have tried" (Section 3). No comparable estimate is given for any other intervention. Mop-ups are reported at 3–6 points, but that is staff impression, not measured on the same basis.

## 3. The 57% → 70% projection ignores the report's own Section 4

Even if reminders do work, they would likely work less well in the non-reminder schools:

- **Reach:** with valid mobiles for only 61% of families, about two in five non-consenting families could not receive a text at all.
- **Language:** if the messages and portal are English-only, they may not land with the families least likely to consent.
- **Incomplete forms:** reminders prompt people to return a form. They do not fix forms returned with the medical history blank.
- **Comparison point:** the 70% reached in western schools reflects their nurses and demographics as well as reminders. "Bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" assumes those differences disappear.

The 70% Eastvale-wide target therefore looks optimistic. Given the corrected baseline of 62.4%, the gap to close is also larger than the report implies.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Families vs pupils.** Section 5 says "about 4,990 families", but 4,990 is the number of *pupils* without consent. Siblings mean fewer families, so the cost is if anything overstated, which is harmless but should be labelled correctly.
- **Reminder-school cost uses a post-reminder count.** The £550 figure uses the 2,280 pupils still without consent at the end, but texts went to everyone without consent at the start, a larger number. The real cost is somewhat higher, though still small.
- **No baseline.** The report does not say what uptake these 38 schools had in 2024-25, before reminders. That is the most obvious missing analysis (see below).
- **Mop-up sessions** are raised in Section 4 but dropped from the recommendation, even though they target the same families reminders struggle to reach.

## 5. Suggestions

**Strengthen the analysis with data you likely already hold:**
1. **Before-and-after comparison.** Compare each school's change from 2024-25 to 2025-26 for reminder and non-reminder schools. A larger rise in reminder schools would be much better evidence than the raw gap.
2. **Like-for-like comparison.** Compare uptake within groups of similar schools, for example nurse vs no nurse, or by deprivation quintile or ward.
3. **Within-school comparison.** Check whether consent return among families who received texts rose faster in the reminder window than among families without a valid mobile.

**Reframe the recommendation.** The low cost is a strong argument, and does not depend on claiming a 13-point effect. Something like:

> "Reminders are very cheap (under £5,000 in year one) and associated with higher consent return. We recommend extending them to all schools, alongside work to improve mobile number coverage, translated messages, and more mop-up sessions in the eastern wards. Rollout should be phased so the effect can be measured."

**Build in evaluation.** If rollout can't happen everywhere at once, introduce reminders to schools in a random order (a stepped rollout). That gives a reliable estimate of the effect for 2026-27 at almost no extra cost.

## Bottom line

Extending reminders is probably still worth doing, because the cost is trivial. But the report should:
- correct overall uptake to 62.4% and drop the claim that the 65% ambition was met;
- describe the 13 points as an association, not a measured effect;
- present a more cautious projection that reflects the contact-data and language barriers it already identifies.
